findings.title: No DMARC record
findings.explain: Receiving mail servers get no instruction about forged mail that claims to come from this domain, so most will deliver it.
findings.fix: Publish a TXT record at _dmarc.<domain>. Start with p=none and a rua address to collect reports, then move to quarantine and reject once every legitimate sender passes.

findings.title: More than one DMARC record
findings.explain: When a domain publishes two DMARC records, receivers are required to ignore both. The domain is effectively unprotected.
findings.fix: Merge them into one TXT record at _dmarc.<domain> and delete the other.

findings.title: DMARC record can't be read
findings.explain: The record exists but receivers can't use it, usually because v=DMARC1 is not the first tag or the p tag is missing or misspelled.
findings.fix: Rewrite the record so it starts with v=DMARC1 followed by p=none, p=quarantine or p=reject.

findings.title: DMARC is in monitoring mode
findings.explain: p=none asks receivers to deliver forged mail as normal and only send reports. It is the right first step, not a place to stay.
findings.fix: Read the aggregate reports, make sure every service that sends as this domain passes SPF or DKIM, then change p=none to p=quarantine.

findings.title: Forged mail goes to spam, not refused
findings.explain: p=quarantine tells receivers to treat failing mail as suspicious, usually by filing it as spam. Recipients can still find and open it.
findings.fix: Once reports show no legitimate mail failing, change p=quarantine to p=reject.

findings.title: Policy applies to only part of the mail
findings.explain: A pct value below 100 means the policy is applied to only that percentage of failing messages. The rest are treated as if the policy were one step weaker.
findings.fix: Raise pct to 100, or remove the tag, since 100 is the default.

findings.title: Subdomains are less protected than the main domain
findings.explain: The sp tag sets a weaker policy for subdomains, so forged mail from made-up subdomains such as billing.example.ca is treated more leniently.
findings.fix: Set sp to the same value as p, or remove sp so subdomains inherit p.

findings.title: No address for DMARC reports
findings.explain: Without a rua address the domain owner never sees who is sending mail in its name, which makes it hard to tighten the policy safely.
findings.fix: Add rua=mailto: with a mailbox or a reporting service you control.

findings.title: Report address on another domain is not authorized
findings.explain: Reports are addressed to a different domain, and that domain has not published the record saying it accepts them. Many receivers will skip sending reports there.
findings.fix: Ask the owner of the report domain to publish <your-domain>._report._dmarc.<their-domain> TXT "v=DMARC1".

findings.title: Forged mail is refused
findings.explain: p=reject applies to all failing mail. Receivers that honour DMARC will refuse messages that forge this domain.

findings.title: No SPF record
findings.explain: The domain doesn't list which servers are allowed to send its mail, so SPF can never pass. DMARC then depends entirely on DKIM.
findings.fix: Publish one TXT record at the domain listing your mail providers, ending in -all or ~all.

findings.title: More than one SPF record
findings.explain: Two records starting with v=spf1 cause a permanent error, so SPF fails for every message.
findings.fix: Combine the mechanisms into a single record and delete the other.

findings.title: SPF needs more than 10 DNS lookups
findings.explain: Counting every include, a, mx, ptr, exists and redirect, including those inside included records, the total is over 10. Receivers return a permanent error and SPF fails.
findings.fix: Remove services you no longer use, replace a and mx with ip4 and ip6 ranges where they are stable, or move some senders to a subdomain.

findings.title: SPF points at names that don't exist
findings.explain: More than two lookups in the record return no answer. Receivers may treat this as a permanent error.
findings.fix: Remove includes and hostnames that no longer resolve.

findings.title: SPF includes a record that isn't there
findings.explain: An include points to a domain that has no SPF record. That is a permanent error, so SPF fails for every message.
findings.fix: Fix the hostname in the include or remove it.

findings.title: SPF allows every server on the internet
findings.explain: +all tells receivers that any server may send for this domain, which defeats the purpose of SPF.
findings.fix: Change +all to -all or ~all.

findings.title: SPF makes no claim about other servers
findings.explain: ?all, or a record with no all at all, says nothing about servers not listed. Mail from them is neither passed nor failed.
findings.fix: End the record with -all or ~all.

findings.title: SPF uses softfail
findings.explain: ~all marks unlisted servers as suspicious rather than failing them. With DMARC at quarantine or reject this is common and acceptable. -all is the stricter choice.
findings.fix: Optional: change ~all to -all once you are sure every sender is listed.

findings.title: SPF uses the ptr mechanism
findings.explain: ptr is slow, unreliable and discouraged by the SPF standard. Some receivers ignore it.
findings.fix: Replace ptr with ip4, ip6 or include entries.

findings.title: No mail servers listed
findings.explain: The domain has no MX records, so it probably doesn't receive mail. It can still be forged as a sender.
findings.fix: If the domain never sends mail, see NON_MAIL_DOMAIN_OPEN.

findings.title: Domain declares it takes no mail
findings.explain: A null MX record tells senders this domain never accepts mail. It's the correct setup for a domain used only for a website.

findings.title: Domain doesn't use email but can still be forged
findings.explain: The domain has no mail servers or a null MX, but hasn't published v=spf1 -all and p=reject. Attackers favour domains like this because nobody watches them.
findings.fix: Publish v=spf1 -all at the domain and v=DMARC1; p=reject at _dmarc.

findings.title: No MTA-STS policy
findings.explain: Other mail servers aren't told to require an encrypted connection when delivering to this domain. This is about privacy in transit, not spoofing.
findings.fix: Publish _mta-sts.<domain> TXT and a policy file at https://mta-sts.<domain>/.well-known/mta-sts.txt, starting in testing mode.

findings.title: MTA-STS is in testing mode
findings.explain: The policy is published but senders only report problems instead of refusing unencrypted delivery.
findings.fix: Change mode: testing to mode: enforce once TLS reports are clean.

findings.title: MTA-STS policy file can't be fetched
findings.explain: The TXT record says a policy exists, but the policy file did not load over HTTPS. Senders will ignore MTA-STS.
findings.fix: Check that https://mta-sts.<domain>/.well-known/mta-sts.txt loads with a valid certificate.

findings.title: No TLS reporting address
findings.explain: The domain won't hear about failed encrypted deliveries.
findings.fix: Publish _smtp._tls.<domain> TXT "v=TLSRPTv1; rua=mailto:tls-reports@<domain>".

findings.title: DKIM key found
findings.explain: A DKIM public key was found at one of the common selectors, so at least one sender signs mail for this domain.

findings.title: DKIM not found at common selectors
findings.explain: DKIM keys can only be found if you know the selector name, and none of the common ones answered. This does not mean DKIM is missing.

findings.title: Domain doesn't exist
findings.explain: DNS says this domain doesn't exist. The inventory entry is probably wrong.
findings.fix: Check the domain against the organization's official website and correct data/inventory.csv.

findings.title: DNS didn't answer in time
findings.explain: The lookup timed out, so this result is incomplete. The next scan will try again.
